title: Y. Kuper
summary: Named in a Zionist territorialist entry.

enrichment.markdown:
**Y. Kuper (י. קופער)**

No reliable person-level record was found for Y. Kuper under **Kuper, Cooper, Kupper, Kopper, Koper**, or the Hebrew/Yiddish forms **קופער / קופר** in the searched JewishGen, Yad Vashem, USHMM, and KehilaLinks materials. The initial is too limited to distinguish this person from other Kuper/Kupper families. No birth, death, migration, occupation, or wartime fate can therefore be assigned with confidence.

**Y. B. Eisenstein**

The Drohiczyn material confirms that Eisenstein was an important family and community name: the memorial-book project lists **Dovid Eisenstein** as chairman and **Hersh Leib Eisenstein** as treasurer, while the KehilaLinks site was compiled by **Benjamin M. Eisenstein**. These are evidence of continuing Eisenstein involvement in documenting the community, but they do not establish that any of them was the **Y. B. Eisenstein** connected with Kuper. ([JewishGen memorial-book portal](https://jewishgen.org/yizkor/Drohichyn/Drogichin.html); [KehilaLinks](https://kehilalinks.jewishgen.org/drogicin/drogicin.html)) ([jewishgen.org](https://jewishgen.org/yizkor/Drohichyn/Drogichin.html?utm_source=openai))

**Shmuel Fishman**

JewishGen preserves a first-person account by Shmuel Fishman describing his arrival as a wartime refugee near Drohiczyn in late 1916 and his work with young local Jews in German forced labor. He portrays the town’s young intellectuals as Hebraists and enthusiastic Zionists, and records an episode in which he sought permission to mark the Balfour Declaration. This places Fishman within the town’s post-World War I Zionist environment, although the source gives no verified family connection to Kuper or Eisenstein. ([Fishman’s Drohiczyn account](https://jewishgen.org/yizkor/Drohichyn/dro265.html)) ([jewishgen.org](https://jewishgen.org/yizkor/Drohichyn/dro265.html?utm_source=openai))

**Zionist organizations**

The outside material supports the broader setting of the entry. Drohiczyn had an active Jewish public sphere before the Holocaust, including Hebrew and Yiddish education, a Tarbut school, a Talmud Torah, and a Kultur Lige branch. The available archives do not identify a Drohiczyn-specific membership list for the **Zionist Territorialists**, **First Zionist Organization**, or **Bund**, nor do they name Kuper as an officer. ([Yad Vashem community history](https://collections.yadvashem.org/en/untold-stories/community/14622229)) ([collections.yadvashem.org](https://collections.yadvashem.org/en/untold-stories/community/14622229?utm_source=openai))

**People’s Library, People’s House, People’s Bank, and Centos**

I found no archive page securely identifying these Drohiczyn institutions by name or linking them to Kuper. Their presence is consistent with the town’s extensive civic, educational, financial, and mutual-aid infrastructure, but the searched sources do not supply addresses, founding dates, personnel, or surviving records for them.

The community context is well documented: approximately 1,500 Jews lived in Drohiczyn between the wars, and most were artisans or merchants. German occupation brought forced labor, ghettoization, and mass deportations and killings in 1942; no source located here connects Kuper personally to those events. ([Yad Vashem](https://collections.yadvashem.org/en/untold-stories/community/14622229)) ([wwv.yadvashem.org](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=257&utm_source=openai))
